turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this computer's playing up. Give me a moment. What's brought you in today?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's the wound, doc. After the hernia. It's gone red and there's gunk coming out of it.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hernia repair, right. I'm opening the letter now. When was the operation?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten days ago. Open repair, right groin. It was a Tuesday.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say that again? The screen just jumped back a page.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten days back. Right side, in the groin.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did the redness start?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. A few days. Could've been three, could've been four. I wasn't clocking it.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hang on, I'm still stuck in someone else's notes. Is there discharge?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yellowish. Not a heap, just a bit down the bottom end. Smells a bit off, if I'm honest.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): And it's sore. Throbs when I walk. If I sit it eases off.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): How bad's the pain, out of ten?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Six? Six out of ten, something like that.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any temperature?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Last night I was shivering. The thermometer said thirty eight point two... no, thirty eight point six. My wife checked it twice.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shivery sitting here?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Not right this minute. I still feel a bit warm though.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, I'll get the dressing off and have a look. One second.

[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Redness about four centimetres round the stitches in the right groin, with yellow discharge at the lower end. Edges are together, not gaping, and it's tender to press. No red tracking up the belly, and I can't feel a pocket of pus.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Worse than yesterday, hey.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's angry, yes. Any vomiting, or diarrhoea?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Bowels have been fine. No spewing.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the waterworks? Burning, or going more often?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, all normal there.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Chest wise, short of breath, any cough?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Breathing's alright.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any bleeding from the wound?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): No blood. Just that yellow stuff.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, a message popped up, I missed that. No blood, you said?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, no blood.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): What medicines did they send you home with?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Those pink capsules. Keflex, I think that's what was on the box. For the wound.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's cephalexin. What dose were you on?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Five hundred milligrams, by mouth. I thought it was three times a day... no, four times a day. Yeah. Four.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days was the course?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days... or was it seven. I don't know, doctor. The packet's on the bench at home.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Say again? Five or seven?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I honestly don't know. I finished the lot a couple of days ago. Didn't miss any while I had them.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): And for pain?

[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Panadol, two tablets by mouth when it hurts. They also gave me Endone. I was taking ten milligrams... no, five milligrams, twice a day. Stopped it, made me sick in the stomach.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): When did you stop the Endone?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days ago. Haven't had one since.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any regular tablets? Blood pressure, anything like that?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): The water tablet. Little white one. I don't know the name, doctor. One every morning, for my blood pressure. Been on it five-ish years.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, so the blood pressure is ongoing, and the file hasn't got the tablet name either. You're sure you don't know it?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No idea. The chemist just says my water tablet.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?

[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Years ago they said penicillin. I came up in a rash as a kid. I'm not even sure it was a real allergy. Mum reckoned, but I never saw anything written down.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): So a possible penicillin rash, not confirmed. The Keflex is a cousin of penicillin. Any rash with those pink capsules?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No rash from them.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Before the op, any blood tests they commented on?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): They said my sugar was borderline. No actual number. Dad was diabetic, so they were fussed. That's all I was told.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): I won't chase a number we don't have. I'll swab the wound today and change the antibiotic, seeing the Keflex is finished and it's still angry.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I have to go back into hospital? Parking there's a shocker, and the grandkids are over this arvo.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. Nothing to drain. My working thought is a superficial wound infection. I can't fully rule out a small deeper collection.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. So what am I taking?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Doxycycline. I'll put fifty milligrams... no, a hundred milligrams, by mouth, twice a day, for seven days.

[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Take it with food and stay upright for half an hour after. Don't restart the Keflex. Stick with the Panadol, leave the Endone alone. Keep the wound clean and dry, new dressing once a day, no soaking it in the bath.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): Hundred milligrams, twice a day, seven days. Yep.

[SEG0060] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads, or you're shivering again, or the ooze gets heavy, go to emergency. Otherwise I'll see you back here in three days to check the swab and the wound.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): Three days. What about work? I'm a sparky. Been off since the op.
[SEG0062] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay off until I review you. No lifting.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke, if you're writing that down. Couple of beers of a Saturday usually. Haven't had one since the operation, mind you.

[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Noted. Pulse was seventy eight... no, that's the pre-op one, today it's ninety two. Blood pressure is one thirty six over eighty four, temperature thirty seven point four. Oxygen sats are ninety eight percent.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety two bad?

[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): A bit high, which fits an infection, and you're not spiking now at thirty seven point four. Swab goes off today, script will be at your chemist. We won't guess whether it was five days or seven. See you in three days.

clinical_actions.description: Wound swab

Start doxycycline 100 mg by mouth twice a day for 7 days; prescription will be at the chemist

Do not restart Keflex
Continue Panadol for pain and do not take Endone

spec.situation: Patient 10 days after a hernia, appendix or caesarean operation; wound redness and discharge, fever the night before; nurse removes dressing and describes it; patient is vague about antibiotic course ('five days... or was it seven'); wound swab and antibiotic change.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats

bad.reason: Last-night fever supported, but not clearly current; now not shivery, only feels warm.
bad.text: fever (category=constitutional, status=present, onset=last night, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Cough was asked about, but patient only said breathing was alright.
Doxycycline regimen supported, but indication stated as wound infection, not explicitly superficial wound infection.

bad.reason: Shortness of breath denied, but cough not explicitly denied.

omissions.text: Wound discharge was described by the patient as smelling 'a bit off'.
The patient had no missed doses of cephalexin while taking it and finished the course a couple of days ago; the prescribed course length was uncertain between 5 and 7 days.
Endone 5 mg was stopped 3 days ago, and the patient has not taken any since.
The regular blood pressure 'water tablet' is taken by mouth one every morning.
On examination, the wound edges were together/not gaping around the stitches in the right groin.
The doctor stated there was nothing to drain and that hospital admission was not needed today.
The patient was advised that the follow-up in 3 days was to check both the wound swab result and the wound itself.
The wound swab was said to be sent off the same day, and the doxycycline prescription would be sent to the patient's chemist.
